Yes. 

Despite the brevity of the story, the two main characters—Ilse and her son Jonas—are given remarkable psychological depth and complexity through subtle details, subtext, and brief glimpses into their shared past. 

Ilse is portrayed as stoic, stubborn, and deeply attached to her routine and independence (wiping a railing that will immediately get wet again, insisting on making one last crossing for what might just be a wooden post, and keeping her son at arm's length). Yet, her memories of Jonas as a boy and her late partner Henning ("Irgendwann hatte der Regen es getan") reveal a quiet grief and deep-seated affection beneath her gruff exterior. Her final action—handing Jonas the mooring line—shows a subtle shift in her character, allowing him in and accepting his help in the only way she knows how.

Jonas is equally well-realized as a child who has moved away to a more modern, urban life—evidenced by his impractical rain jacket, light-soled shoes, rolling suitcase, and habit of making color-coded spreadsheets—who nonetheless understands his mother's defenses intimately ("Dann hättest du gesagt, es passt gerade nicht") and returns out of concern for her and the failing ferry business. 

Even the minor, "flat" characters (the two polite cyclists and the mentioned Henning) are used at the exact right level of complexity for a very short story; they ground the setting in reality and highlight the dynamic between the mother and son without feeling like artificial plot devices.
